newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl seeks to crush speculation on EMU delay.
newsitem.headline: Kohl seeks to crush speculation on EMU delay.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl, seeking to crush growing speculation that European monetary union may be delayed, said on Sunday that Germany would qualify on time for the new single currency without softening the entry rules.

Kohl said delaying the euro, set to be launched on January 1, 1999, could prove fatal to the project and would cause the mark to rise against the dollar and other European currencies, wiping out a recent decline that had helped Germany's export-driven economy to recover.
"The criteria in the Maastricht Treaty are not up for discussion," Kohl said in a speech opening an international chemical industry conference in Frankfurt.
He said a delay in introducing the euro, his pet project, could mean that it was delayed forever. "Those who are thinking about a delay might consider the impact on the mark," he added.

Debate about a delay, previously a taboo subject in Bonn, flared up last week when Finance Minister Theo Waigel was forced to retreat from his plan for revaluing the Bundesbank's gold and currency stocks to help to plug a shortfall of at least 19 billion marks ($11 billion) in his 1997 budget.
Economists predict slow economic growth and high jobless rates will mean Germany cannot join EMU since it would fail to meet the Maastricht critieria as Waigel interprets them.

Waigel, who faces stiff opposition from Kohl's junior coalition partners, the Free Democrats (FDP), to tax rises, has said he will not resort to increasing taxes to fill the deficit -- at least not this year when nations wanting to join the new currency must meet the entry criteria.

Kohl strongly backed Waigel, saying Germany would meet the most controversial criteria which requires a budget deficit of 3.0 percent or less of Gross Domestic Product (GDP). He also predicted 1997 economic growth of at least 2.5 percent.

Critics of Waigel say the treaty states the deficit must be "three percent" or less, leaving room for interpretation that nations with a deficit slightly above 3.0 percent should also be allowed into EMU.
But Waigel, who was in Luxembourg on Sunday for a meeting of European Union finance ministers, promised earlier that Germany would qualify without tricks.

"You will see, Germany will make the deficit criteria," he told journalists at a weekend meeting of the junior wing of his Christian Social Union (CSU), Bavarian sister party to Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU).
Several senior figures have suggested that a looser interpretation of entry rules would be preferable to a delay to the euro project.
"The convergence criteria are not mathematical (goals), but rather psychological," Karl Lamers, the CDU foreign policy spokesman, told Berlin's Tagesspiegel newspaper.

Martin Kohlhaussen, president of the Federal Association of German Banks, told the Frankfurter Allgemeine Sonntagszeitung that Germany should enter EMU in 1999 even if its deficit was as high as 3.3 percent of GDP.
"I would hope that Waigel moves a bit away from his goal of a pin-point landing," said Kohlhaussen, who is also president of Commerzbank AG, one of the country's top commercial banks.

But Waigel, under pressure from his conservative CSU party to stick to a water-tight interpretation, said the German public would not accept any currency less stable than the mark, a symbol of post-war Germany's economic recovery.
Further signs of discontent in Germany about currency union, particularly if Italy and Spain were allowed to join due to softer entry criteria, emerged at the weekend.
A poll in Focus magazine said 82 percent of Germans surveyed in an IRNA poll said they wanted EMU delayed if member countries could not meet entry criteria strictly.

Several thousand people took to the streets of Munich, Waigel's home region, on Saturday to protest against the government's welfare policies and spending cuts imposed to help Germany to qualify for EMU.

But former European Commission president Jaques Delors told Focus that a delay to EMU would be disastrous. "Even only a one year delay to the start of the currency union would be the end of the project," he said.
